sections.normalized_html:
In a right triangle, the cosine of an angle is defined as the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse.

In the given triangle, the adjacent side to [MATH: \theta] has length [MATH: 4.]

To find the hypotenuse, [MATH: c,] we apply the Pythagorean Theorem: [MATH: c^{2}|= 3^{2} + 4^{2}; c^{2}|= 9 + 16; c^{2}|= 25; c|= sqrt(25); c|= 5]

Thus, [MATH: \cos \theta = \dfrac{4}{5}.]

sections.normalized_html:
In a right triangle, the sine of an angle is defined as the ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse.

In the given triangle, the hypotenuse has length [MATH: 5,] and the adjacent side to [MATH: \theta] has length [MATH: 4.]

The side opposite [MATH: \theta] is unknown, so we apply the Pythagorean Theorem to solve for it:

[MATH: 5^{2}|= 4^{2} + x^{2}; 25|= 16 + x^{2}; x^{2}|= 9; x|= sqrt(9); x|= 3]

Thus, [MATH: \sin \theta = \dfrac{3}{5}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Trigonometry problems sometimes require us to find a missing side or trigonometric ratio when only two sides of a right triangle are given. These questions test the ability to connect the Pythagorean theorem with sine, cosine, and tangent definitions.

Content:
In this lesson, we’ll practice using the Pythagorean theorem to complete missing triangle information and then find trigonometric ratios.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Cosine of an Angle Given the Legs of a Right Triangle

Example Prompt:
In the triangle shown, what is the value of [MATH: \cos \theta?]

[IMG: /graphics/7c9c19729abcdda1d9a3274f8139dd3b]

(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
In a right triangle, the cosine of an angle is defined as the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse.

In the given triangle, the adjacent side to [MATH: \theta] has length [MATH: 4.]

To find the hypotenuse, [MATH: c,] we apply the Pythagorean Theorem:
[MATH: c^{2}|= 3^{2} + 4^{2}; c^{2}|= 9 + 16; c^{2}|= 25; c|= sqrt(25); c|= 5]

Thus,
[MATH: \cos \theta = \dfrac{4}{5}.]
